summary:
Laos has never criminalised consensual same-sex conduct. Human Dignity Trust records that Laos, together with Cambodia, gained independence from France in the 1950s and modelled its penal code on the French system, which contains no sodomy offence; neighbouring states that retained colonial prohibitions did not follow that route.

The visitor-facing risk is legal vacuum rather than prosecution. There is no legal gender recognition procedure, no constitutional provision addressing sexual orientation or gender identity, and no statute prohibiting discrimination on those grounds. At the 35th session of the Universal Periodic Review on 21 January 2020, the ambassadors of Malta and Iceland recommended that Laos improve LGBTI rights with LGBTI representatives involved in decision-making and adopt comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity; the inventory records no such legislation.

Partial movement exists inside the legislature. In March 2025, National Assembly member Maifong Maixai proposed amending Article 36 of the 2025 revised Constitution to widen the space for non-discrimination protections for gender-diverse people. Whether the amendment was adopted is not established in these sources.

One statutory protection does reach the visitor: the Law on Electronic Data Protection (No. 25/NA, 12 May 2017) lists sexual behaviour among the categories of data that are prohibited from processing.

State tolerance is conditional. The government generally ignores LGBTQ people unless they campaign for rights or are judged publicly immodest or indecent, and a 2014 decree prohibited criticism of government policies. A 2018 Al Jazeera investigation described a tightening of state attention to social media, with influential Facebook users facing retribution for posts, and reported the blocking of LGBTQ-themed webpages. Discussion of LGBTQ issues in Laotian media is rare apart from transsexual people appearing as entertainment.

Visibility is nonetheless concrete. A 2000 first-person account from Vientiane found a small circle of lesbian and gay people whose social life centred on a few restaurants and friendship networks. Transgender people attend temples and ceremonies in traditional costume, and the first public Pride in Laos drew about 100 participants in June 2012, held on the United States embassy sports field in Vientiane. The country's single LGBT advocacy group, Proud to be us Laos, was quoted in the 2018 reporting, and the European Union marked the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia in Vientiane, giving LGBT rights visible diplomatic backing.

For a trans visitor the dominant exposure is administrative: a passport that does not match presentation can be challenged by an opaque bureaucracy with no anti-discrimination remedy and no independent civil society, since the one-party system leaves no separate body to appeal to.
tangentialFactors:
Criminalisation is the clearest axis on which Laos differs from its neighbourhood. Where several regional neighbours kept colonial sodomy provisions, the French-derived Laotian code did not carry them forward, so a trans or gay visitor should expect no consensual-conduct offence to be charged.

Discrimination outside the statute is documented. Gay foreigners reported in the 1990s that a social taboo made interaction with Laotians difficult except discreetly at night, and the United States Department of State reported in 2013 that societal discrimination against LGBT people and against people living with HIV/AIDS was prevalent. Practically, hostility is expressed through discretion and social avoidance rather than arrest.

Political context shapes what advocacy can do. The 2014 decree barring criticism of government policy, combined with the 2018 pressure on prominent social-media users, means that public campaigning carries a risk that ordinary private conduct does not. The age of consent is 15 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity, so age-of-consent law is not a differentiating hazard.

Diplomatic presence provides limited cover. The European Union's observance of the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia in Vientiane and the hosting of the 2012 Pride on the United States embassy grounds indicate that foreign missions will mark and stage LGBT events, while the domestic scene remains small, discreet and centred on private networks rather than institutions.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution does not expressly address either. The 2020 Universal Periodic Review recommendations from Malta and Iceland called for comprehensive legislation covering both grounds; no such law appears in the sources.

In March 2025, National Assembly member Maifong Maixai proposed changing Article 36 of the 2025 revised Constitution to expand the room available for non-discrimination protections for gender-diverse people.

The Law on Electronic Data Protection (No. 25/NA, 12 May 2017) classifies sexual behaviour as a prohibited data category, giving residents a formal constraint on the collection and processing of that information.

Advocacy operates under constraint. Proud to be us Laos is identified as the country's only LGBT advocacy group, and it functions amid a 2014 decree prohibiting criticism of government policies and a documented 2018 crackdown on influential social-media users. Health-sector institutions involved in LGBT-related events include the Center for HIV/AIDS/STI (CHAS) at the Lao Ministry of Health, the Lao Positive Health Association, and the Vientiane Youth Center for Health and Development, which helped organise the first public Pride in June 2012 with around 100 participants.

Everyday visibility exists in specific registers: activist Anan Bouapha has described gay students expressing themselves among peers and teachers, and transgender people wearing traditional costume at temples and ceremonies. Public media discussion of LGBTQ issues remains rare, with trans people appearing mainly as entertainment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced account of a legal gender recognition procedure in Laos. The absence of any such framework is asserted in the current record but not evidenced by a statute, regulation or court decision in these sources, and remains to be verified against the current penal, civil-status and family legislation.

Whether the March 2025 proposal to amend Article 36 of the revised Constitution was adopted, and in what wording, is unresolved.

Whether the two 2020 Universal Periodic Review recommendations on anti-discrimination legislation were accepted or implemented is not established here.

No source in this inventory addresses school policy, bullying, education-specific protections for LGBTQ youth, or healthcare access for trans people and trans youth. Those gaps are not findings of absence.

Entry, visa and border-screening practice for passports that do not match a traveller's presentation, and any specific document-checking behaviour at Wattay International Airport, are not documented in these sources.
